title: Smoky Vegan Split Pea Soup
description: A pound of split peas, a few vegetables and smoked paprika make a thick, savory pot that feeds eight for about $1 a bowl. No ham needed, and it freezes flat in bags for months.
equipment: 6-quart or larger pot or Dutch oven
notes: The soup is done when the peas have collapsed into a thick purée; older split peas take longer, so give them time and add water as needed. For a non-vegan version, render 4 slices of chopped thick-cut bacon in the pot before the onion. Cool the soup quickly by dividing it into shallow containers and refrigerate within 2 hours; it keeps 5 days in the refrigerator. For the freezer, portion into 2-cup freezer bags, press flat, and freeze up to 4 months. Thaw overnight in the refrigerator or run the sealed bag under warm water to loosen, then reheat in a pot over medium-low with a splash of water, stirring, until steaming and 165°F throughout. In the microwave, heat in a covered bowl, stirring halfway. The soup thickens as it sits; thin with hot water to the texture you like.

ingredients.name: green split peas (450 g), rinsed and picked over
yukon gold potatoes, peeled and cut into 1/2-inch dice
kosher salt, plus more to taste
chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley, for serving

instructions: Warm the olive oil in a 6-quart pot over medium heat. Add the onion, carrots, celery and 1/2 teaspoon of the salt and cook, stirring now and then, until the vegetables are soft and the onion is translucent, 8 to 10 minutes.
Stir in the garlic, smoked paprika, thyme, cumin and red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Add the split peas, potatoes, bay leaves, broth, water and the remaining 1 teaspoon salt. Bring to a boil over high heat, then reduce the heat to low so the soup barely simmers and partially cover the pot.

Simmer, stirring every 10 to 15 minutes and scraping the bottom so the peas do not catch, until the peas have fully broken down and the soup is thick, 60 to 75 minutes. If it gets too thick to stir easily, add hot water 1/2 cup at a time.

Remove the bay leaves. Stir in the mustard, vinegar and frozen peas and simmer 2 minutes more. Taste and add salt and pepper as needed; for a smoother texture, blend a few cups of the soup with an immersion blender and stir it back in.
Ladle into bowls and top with parsley. Leftovers thicken as they cool, so loosen with a little hot water when reheating.

title: Big-Batch Vegetable Minestrone with Cannellini Beans
description: An Italian-style vegetable soup built on canned tomatoes, two cans of beans and whatever sturdy vegetables are cheap that week. Eight dinner bowls for about $1.50 each; the pasta cooks separately so the soup freezes cleanly.
notes: Swap in what you have: green beans, frozen corn kernels, kale or a diced sweet potato all work in place of the zucchini or cabbage. Grated parmesan or a parmesan rind simmered in the pot adds depth but adds milk and makes the soup no longer vegan. Keep the cooked pasta in its own container; stored in the soup it swells and turns soft. Refrigerate within 2 hours; the soup keeps 4 days and the pasta 3 days. Freeze the soup without pasta in 2-cup containers or flat bags up to 4 months, thaw overnight in the refrigerator, and reheat in a pot over medium heat, stirring, until it reaches 165°F, then add freshly cooked pasta. The soup thickens as the potatoes and beans sit; thin with water or broth when reheating.

ingredients.name: yukon gold potatoes, cut into 1/2-inch dice
cannellini beans (15 oz each), drained and rinsed
kosher salt, plus more to taste
fresh basil leaves, torn, for serving

instructions: Heat the olive oil in an 8-quart pot over medium heat. Add the onion, carrots, celery and 1 teaspoon of the salt and cook, stirring occasionally, until softened, 8 to 10 minutes.
Stir in the garlic, oregano, red pepper flakes (if using) and tomato paste and cook, stirring, until the paste darkens a shade, 1 to 2 minutes.

Add the crushed tomatoes, broth, water, bay leaves, potatoes and cabbage. Bring to a boil, then reduce the heat to a steady simmer, partially cover and cook until the potatoes are nearly tender, about 15 minutes.
Add the zucchini and beans and simmer, uncovered, until every vegetable is tender and the broth has taken on the color of the tomatoes, 10 to 12 minutes more.

Meanwhile, bring a medium pot of salted water to a boil and cook the ditalini until just shy of tender, about 1 minute less than the package time. Drain and toss with a teaspoon of olive oil so it does not clump.
Remove the bay leaves. Stir the spinach into the soup until it wilts, about 1 minute, then taste and season with the remaining salt and the pepper.
To serve, put a scoop of pasta in each bowl and ladle the hot soup over it. Finish with basil. Store any leftover pasta separately from the soup.

title: Chicken Noodle Soup from Bone-In Thighs
description: Bone-in thighs make their own rich broth while they simmer, so one inexpensive package feeds eight for about $2 a bowl. The noodles cook separately so the soup freezes without turning to mush.
notes: Chicken is safe when the thickest part reads 165°F on an instant-read thermometer; with thighs simmered this long it will be well past that and falling off the bone. Dried spaghetti is the cheapest noodle, but any pasta or egg noodle works; for a gluten-free soup, use rice noodles and gluten-free low-sodium chicken broth. Frozen peas and diced carrots can replace the fresh carrots to save chopping. Keep cooked noodles in their own container so they do not soak up all the broth. Refrigerate within 2 hours; the soup keeps 4 days and the noodles 3 days. Freeze the soup without noodles in 2-cup portions up to 3 months, thaw overnight in the refrigerator, reheat in a pot until it reaches 165°F, and add freshly cooked noodles to each bowl.

ingredients.name: dried spaghetti (225 g), broken into 2-inch lengths

instructions: Pat the chicken thighs dry and season them with 1 teaspoon of the salt. Heat the oil in an 8-quart pot over medium-high heat. Brown the thighs skin side down, in two batches so they are not crowded, until deep golden, 5 to 6 minutes, then transfer to a plate. Pour off all but 2 tablespoons of fat.
Reduce the heat to medium. Add the onion, carrots, celery and 1/2 teaspoon salt and cook, stirring, until softened, 6 to 8 minutes. Add the garlic and thyme and cook 1 minute more.

Return the thighs and any juices to the pot and add the bay leaves, broth and water. Bring to a boil, skim off any foam, then reduce to a gentle simmer, partially cover and cook until the chicken reaches 165°F and pulls easily from the bone, 35 to 40 minutes.

Lift the thighs onto a cutting board and let them cool for 10 minutes. Discard the skin and bones and shred the meat with two forks. While it cools, spoon the excess fat from the surface of the broth.
Meanwhile, bring a medium pot of salted water to a boil and cook the spaghetti pieces until just tender, following the package time. Drain and toss with a little oil.

Return the shredded chicken to the pot along with the peas (if using) and simmer 3 minutes. Remove the bay leaves, stir in the parsley and lemon juice, and season with the remaining salt and the pepper.
Divide the noodles among bowls and ladle the hot soup over them. Serve right away.

title: Creamy Potato and Scallion Soup
description: A potato-leek-style soup made with cheaper onions and two bunches of scallions, blended smooth with a little butter and milk. Eight bowls for under $1 each, and it freezes well because it is puréed.
notes: Cook the onion and scallions slowly without browning so the soup stays pale and sweet. Blend only until smooth; overworking potatoes, especially in a high-speed blender, turns them gluey. For a vegan, dairy-free version, use olive oil instead of butter and unsweetened nut-free plant milk instead of whole milk. Good toppings are extra scallion greens, sharp cheddar cheese, or crumbled thick-cut bacon. Refrigerate within 2 hours and use within 4 days. Puréed potato soups freeze well: cool, portion into containers leaving an inch of headroom, and freeze up to 3 months. Thaw overnight in the refrigerator and reheat gently over medium-low, whisking as it warms until it is smooth and steaming at 165°F; a quick pass with the immersion blender fixes any graininess.

ingredients.name: scallions, white and light green parts sliced, dark green tops thinly sliced and reserved for serving
russet or yukon gold potatoes (about 1.4 kg), peeled and cut into 1-inch chunks
kosher salt, plus more to taste

instructions: Melt the butter in a 6-quart pot over medium-low heat. Add the onion, the white and light green scallion slices and 1/2 teaspoon of the salt. Cook, stirring often, until very soft but not browned, 10 to 12 minutes. Add the garlic and cook 1 minute more.

Add the potatoes, broth, water, bay leaf, thyme sprigs and the remaining 1 teaspoon salt. Bring to a boil, then reduce the heat, cover and simmer until the potatoes fall apart when pressed with a spoon, 20 to 25 minutes.

Remove the bay leaf and thyme stems. Blend with an immersion blender just until smooth, about 1 minute; or blend in batches in a countertop blender, filling it no more than halfway and holding the lid down with a folded towel.
Return the soup to low heat and stir in the milk and lemon juice. Warm until steaming but not boiling, then taste and season with the pepper and more salt if needed.
Ladle into bowls and top with the reserved scallion greens, a grind of pepper and a thin drizzle of olive oil if you like.

title: Pozole-Inspired Red Chile Chicken and Hominy Soup
description: A Mexican-style pot of chicken thighs and hominy in a mild guajillo chile broth, finished at the table with cabbage, radish and lime. Two pounds of thighs stretch to eight bowls for about $2 each.
notes: Guajillo chiles are mild and fruity; toast them only until fragrant, because scorched chiles turn the broth bitter. The chicken is done when it reads 165°F at the thickest part and shreds easily. If you cannot find dried chiles, skip the soaking step and use 3 tablespoons ancho chili powder in total. Hominy holds its chew after freezing, so this soup freezes especially well: cool, refrigerate within 2 hours, and keep 4 days in the refrigerator or 3 months in the freezer in 2-cup portions. Thaw overnight in the refrigerator and reheat in a pot over medium heat, stirring, until it reaches 165°F. Prepare the cabbage, radish, onion and lime fresh each time you serve.

ingredients.name: kosher salt, plus more to taste
dried guajillo chiles, stemmed and seeded
white or yellow hominy (25 oz each), drained and rinsed
thinly sliced green cabbage, for serving
limes, cut into wedges, for serving

instructions: Toast the guajillo chiles in a dry small skillet over medium heat, pressing them flat with a spatula, until fragrant and pliable, about 30 seconds per side; do not let them blacken. Put them in a bowl, cover with 2 cups of very hot water and soak until soft, 15 to 20 minutes.

Meanwhile, season the chicken with 1 teaspoon of the salt. Heat the oil in an 8-quart pot over medium-high heat and brown the thighs in two batches, 3 to 4 minutes per side; they will not be cooked through. Return all the chicken to the pot.

Add the quartered onion, garlic halves, bay leaves, broth and water. Bring to a boil, skim any foam, then reduce to a gentle simmer, partially cover and cook until the chicken reads 165°F and shreds easily, 25 to 30 minutes.

While the chicken simmers, put the soaked chiles in a blender with 1 cup of their soaking water, the ancho chili powder, cumin, oregano and a ladle of broth from the pot. Blend until completely smooth, about 1 minute.

Transfer the chicken to a cutting board and shred it with two forks. Fish out and discard the onion, garlic and bay leaves (squeeze the soft garlic back into the pot first if you like). Pour the chile purée through a fine-mesh strainer into the pot, pressing on the solids, and discard what is left in the strainer.

Add the hominy and the remaining 1 teaspoon salt and simmer, uncovered, so the hominy takes on the chile broth, about 15 minutes. Return the chicken, add the pepper and simmer 5 minutes more. Taste and add salt as needed.
Ladle into bowls and set out the cabbage, radishes, cilantro, diced onion, lime wedges and tortillas so everyone can finish their own.

title: Vietnamese-Inspired Lemongrass Chicken and Rice Soup
description: A brothy chicken and jasmine rice soup scented with lemongrass, ginger and fish sauce, finished with scallions, cilantro and lime. A pound and a half of thighs and a cup of rice make eight bowls for about $1.75 each.
notes: Bruise the lemongrass with the back of a knife before adding it so it releases its perfume; it and the ginger slices are removed before serving. Chicken is safe at 165°F at the thickest part. Gluten-free tamari can stand in for the fish sauce, which removes the fish allergen and adds soy. The rice keeps drinking broth as the soup sits, so leftovers are closer to porridge; thin with water or broth when reheating. Refrigerate within 2 hours and use within 4 days. Freeze in 2-cup portions up to 3 months, thaw overnight in the refrigerator, and reheat in a pot over medium heat with a splash of water, stirring, until it reaches 165°F. Add the scallions, cilantro, chile and lime fresh at serving time.

ingredients.name: lemongrass stalks, tough outer layers removed, bruised and cut into 3-inch lengths
fresh ginger (2-inch piece), peeled and thinly sliced
fish sauce, plus more to taste
kosher salt, plus more to taste
serrano or green chile, thinly sliced

instructions: Heat the oil in a 6-quart pot over medium heat. Add the onion and salt and cook, stirring, until soft, about 5 minutes. Add the lemongrass, ginger and garlic and stir until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Pour in the broth and water and add the whole chicken thighs. Bring to a boil, skim any foam from the surface, then reduce to a gentle simmer and cook until the chicken reads 165°F at the thickest part, 20 to 25 minutes.
Lift the chicken onto a cutting board with tongs and let it rest while you continue. Remove and discard the lemongrass and ginger slices.

Stir the rice and carrots into the simmering broth. Cook, stirring every few minutes so the rice does not stick, until the rice is tender and the soup has thickened slightly but is still brothy, 15 to 18 minutes.
Shred the chicken with two forks and return it to the pot with the fish sauce and pepper. Simmer 3 minutes, then taste and add more fish sauce or salt until the broth tastes savory and well seasoned.
Ladle into bowls and top with scallions, cilantro and chile if using. Squeeze lime over each bowl just before eating.

title: Polish-Style Cabbage and Potato Soup with Bacon
description: A kapusniak-inspired pot: half a head of cabbage, potatoes and carrots simmered with a little bacon, tomato paste and allspice, then sharpened with vinegar. Feeds eight for about $1.25 a bowl.
notes: The pot will look overfull when the cabbage goes in; it collapses within minutes. Traditional kapusniak uses sauerkraut, so if you have it, replace 2 cups of the fresh cabbage with 1 cup of drained sauerkraut and cut the vinegar in half. Leave out the sour cream to keep the soup dairy-free; the bacon can be replaced with 2 tablespoons olive oil and an extra teaspoon of smoked paprika for a vegetarian version (use vegetable broth). Refrigerate within 2 hours and use within 4 days. Freeze without the sour cream in 2-cup portions up to 3 months; the potatoes soften a little but the soup is still good. Thaw overnight in the refrigerator and reheat in a pot over medium heat, stirring, until it reaches 165°F, then add dill and sour cream to each bowl.

ingredients.name: russet or yukon gold potatoes, peeled and cut into 3/4-inch chunks
chopped green cabbage (about 1/2 large head, 2 lb)
kosher salt, plus more to taste
apple cider vinegar, plus more to taste

instructions: Cook the bacon in an 8-quart pot over medium heat, stirring, until browned and the fat has rendered, 6 to 8 minutes. Lift it out with a slotted spoon onto a plate, leaving about 2 tablespoons of fat in the pot.

Add the onion, carrots, celery and 1/2 teaspoon of the salt to the fat and cook, stirring, until softened, about 8 minutes. Stir in the garlic, tomato paste, allspice, thyme and smoked paprika and cook until the paste darkens slightly, 1 to 2 minutes.

Add the potatoes, cabbage, bay leaves, broth, water and the remaining 1 teaspoon salt. Bring to a boil, pushing the cabbage under as it wilts, then reduce the heat, cover and simmer until the potatoes are tender and the cabbage is silky, 25 to 30 minutes.

Remove the bay leaves. Stir the bacon back in along with the vinegar and pepper and simmer 5 minutes more. Taste: the soup should be gently sour and well salted, so add more vinegar or salt as needed.
Ladle into bowls and finish each with a spoonful of sour cream and a sprinkle of dill.

title: Moroccan-Inspired Chickpea and Sweet Potato Stew
description: Three cans of chickpeas, sweet potato and carrots in a warmly spiced tomato broth with cumin, coriander, cinnamon and a handful of raisins. Vegan, eight servings at about $1.50 each, and better on the second day.
notes: Blooming the spices in the oil for a minute before the liquid goes in is what makes the stew taste layered rather than dusty. Serve over rice, or over couscous (which adds wheat). Dried chickpeas cost less: cook 1 1/2 cups (300 g) until tender and use them in place of the cans. Diced butternut squash or russet potatoes can replace the sweet potato. Refrigerate within 2 hours and use within 5 days. Freeze in 2-cup portions up to 4 months, thaw overnight in the refrigerator, and reheat in a pot over medium heat with a splash of water, stirring, until it reaches 165°F. Add the lemon and cilantro after reheating for the brightest flavor.

ingredients.name: sweet potato (about 2 medium), peeled and cut into 3/4-inch chunks
chickpeas (15 oz each), drained and rinsed
kosher salt, plus more to taste

instructions: Heat the olive oil in a 6-quart pot over medium heat. Add the onion and 1/2 teaspoon of the salt and cook, stirring, until soft and golden at the edges, 6 to 8 minutes.

Stir in the garlic, ginger, cumin, coriander, smoked paprika, cinnamon, turmeric, cayenne (if using) and tomato paste. Cook, stirring constantly, until the spices smell toasty and the paste darkens, 1 to 2 minutes.
Add the crushed tomatoes, broth, carrots, sweet potato and the remaining 1 teaspoon salt. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a simmer, partially cover and cook 15 minutes.

Add the chickpeas and raisins and simmer, uncovered, until the sweet potato is tender and the stew has thickened a little, 15 to 20 minutes more. Press a few chickpeas against the side of the pot with your spoon to thicken the broth.
Take the pot off the heat and stir in the lemon juice and pepper. Taste and add salt as needed. Serve in bowls, on its own or over rice, with cilantro scattered on top.

title: Caribbean-Inspired Red Bean and Coconut Stew
description: Inspired by Jamaican stew peas: a pound of dried kidney beans simmered with coconut milk, thyme, allspice, scallions and a whole chile for aroma without much heat. Vegan, eight servings, about $1 a bowl over rice.
notes: Dried kidney beans must be boiled hard for 10 minutes before simmering; this destroys a natural toxin in raw kidney beans, so do not skip it or use a slow cooker on low for this step. Keep the chile whole and unbroken so the stew is fragrant, not fiery; fish it out before serving. In a hurry, use 3 cans (15 oz each) of kidney beans, rinsed, skip the soaking and boiling, and simmer with the vegetables for 25 minutes. Small flour dumplings (spinners) are traditional but add wheat. Refrigerate within 2 hours and use within 4 days. Freeze in 2-cup portions up to 4 months; coconut milk stews may look separated after thawing but come together with stirring. Thaw overnight in the refrigerator and reheat in a pot over medium heat, stirring, until it reaches 165°F. Cook fresh rice to serve.

ingredients.name: dried red kidney beans (450 g), picked over and rinsed
scallions, sliced, a handful of greens reserved for serving
scotch bonnet or habanero chile, left whole
sweet potato, peeled and cut into 1-inch chunks
kosher salt, plus more to taste
hot cooked jasmine rice, for serving

instructions: Put the beans in a large bowl, cover with at least 3 inches of cold water and soak 8 hours or overnight. (For a quick soak, cover with water in the pot, boil 2 minutes, cover and let stand 1 hour.) Drain and rinse.

Return the beans to a 6-quart pot with 8 cups fresh water. Bring to a full rolling boil over high heat and boil hard for 10 minutes, skimming any foam. Reduce the heat to a simmer, partially cover and cook until the beans are tender but still whole, 45 to 60 minutes.

Stir in the coconut oil, onion, scallions, garlic, thyme sprigs, allspice, the whole chile (if using), coconut milk, sweet potato, carrots and salt. Return to a simmer and cook, uncovered, stirring now and then, until the vegetables are tender and the liquid has thickened into a light gravy, 25 to 30 minutes.
Remove the chile and thyme stems. Mash a ladleful of beans against the side of the pot and stir it back in to thicken the stew. Season with the pepper and more salt to taste.
Spoon over hot rice and scatter the reserved scallion greens on top.

title: Brown Lentil Soup with Kale, Cumin and Lemon
description: A pound of brown lentils, carrots, onion and a bunch of kale make eight filling bowls for well under $1 each. Cumin, smoked paprika and a squeeze of lemon keep it from tasting plain. Vegan and freezer-ready.
notes: Brown and green lentils hold their shape, so the soup stays brothy with whole lentils; for a thicker soup, blend a cup or two and stir it back in. Lentils vary in age and cook time, so start checking at 25 minutes and stop when they are tender but not mushy. Baby spinach, collard greens or chopped green cabbage can stand in for the kale. Refrigerate within 2 hours and use within 5 days. Freeze in 2-cup portions up to 4 months; thaw overnight in the refrigerator and reheat in a pot over medium heat with a splash of water, stirring, until it reaches 165°F. Add a fresh squeeze of lemon after reheating, since the brightness fades in the freezer.

ingredients.name: brown or green lentils (450 g), rinsed and picked over
kosher salt, plus more to taste
lacinato or curly kale, stems removed, leaves chopped (about 6 cups)

instructions: Heat the olive oil in a 6-quart pot over medium heat. Add the onion, carrots, celery and 1/2 teaspoon of the salt and cook, stirring occasionally, until softened, about 8 minutes.
Stir in the garlic, cumin, coriander, smoked paprika, red pepper flakes (if using) and tomato paste and cook, stirring, until fragrant and the paste has darkened slightly, 1 to 2 minutes.

Add the lentils, bay leaves, broth, water and the remaining 1 teaspoon salt. Bring to a boil, then reduce the heat to a simmer, partially cover and cook, stirring occasionally, until the lentils are tender but still hold their shape, 30 to 40 minutes. Add hot water if the soup gets thicker than you like.
Stir in the kale and simmer until tender, 5 to 7 minutes. Remove the bay leaves.

Take the pot off the heat and stir in the lemon juice and pepper. Taste and add salt as needed; if you want a thicker soup, blend a cup or two with an immersion blender and stir it back in. Serve hot.
